{"file_path": "<HOME>/claude-kredi-runs/2026-10-22/r6w/diag-nogate/runs/X4-ours-1/repo/PR.md", "content": "# Faster bike availability search

Hi Marta,

## What changed

When a customer picks dates, the app finds which bikes are free. That search was slow once the shop had many bikes and many bookings. It is now much faster, and it gives the same answers as before.

## How much faster

I tested with a shop the size of yours: 400 bikes and 50,000 bookings, searching a 3-day window. I ran the same search on the old and the new code on my own computer.

| | Time per search |
|---|---|
| Before | about 220 to 430 milliseconds (it varied between runs) |
| After | about 1 millisecond |

That is roughly 200 to 400 times faster. The times on your server will be different, but the new search should be much faster there too.

## Why it was slow

For each bike, the old search read through all 50,000 bookings to see if any of them clashed. With 400 bikes that is about 20 million checks. The new search reads the bookings once, notes which bikes are taken, and then lists the others. That is about 50,000 checks.

## What stays the same

- The same bikes are offered for the same dates. In my test the old and new code returned the identical list (370 free bikes).
- Bikes still appear cheapest first. Bikes with the same price appear in order of bike number.
- A bike returned on the morning another customer picks it up still counts as free (back-to-back bookings are allowed).
- The two existing automated tests pass.

## What I did not check

- I did not test on your real server or your real booking data. The test data was made up, so the exact speed-up there may differ.
- I only changed the search. Other slow parts of the app, if any, are not changed.
"}

text:
Availability search is faster, and `PR.md` for Marta is written. I did not commit anything.

- **Fix:** `src/availability.js` used to scan all 50,000 bookings once per bike. It now scans bookings once, notes which bikes clash with the requested dates, and filters the bikes against that list. The sort order is unchanged.
- **Timing:** I benchmarked 400 bikes and 50,000 bookings of made-up data, searching a 3-day window, averaged over 5 repetitions per run. Over three runs the old code took about 220–430 ms per search and the new code about 1 ms. That is roughly 200–400× faster, and the old timings varied a lot between runs.
- **Same results:** On the benchmark data, old and new code returned the identical list of 370 free bikes. The 2 existing tests pass.
- **Not checked:** I did not run it against real data or a real server. `PR.md` says this and gives the timing as a range.
